subtopic: OUTLINE OF BUSINESS TO FOLLOW BUDGET DEBATE

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: OUTLINE OF BUSINESS TO FOLLOW BUDGET DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as requested yesterday I propose to make a very short announcement of the business of the House following the conclusion of the budget debate. We propose, on completion of the budget debate, on Thursday to call the resolution preceding the decennial revision of the Bank Act. It has been the practice in the past, I am told, that the legislation respecting amendment of the Quebec Savings Bank Act goes along with that, since the legislation does not differ as between the different institutions.
When that is completed, on Friday we propose to call the Senate reform legislation and on Monday to call a supply motion. When the supply motion is called on Monday we will ask the House to consider having ten departments entered rather than the usual six. This, of course, would in no way prejudice the full rights respecting the remaining five supply motions or the length of time used. The purpose is merely to have the departments entered with a view, if it can be worked out, to having the estimates referred to committees for detailed examination.

Army Benevolent Fund
Serious allegations were recently made by a number of individuals concerning the operations of the Army Benevolent Fund. After due consideration, the Army Benevolent Fund Board decided that each allegation should be carefully examined. Since the Office of the Auditor General was currently engaged on a mid-year, or interim, audit of the Fund's records, the Board asked the Auditor General to enlarge the scope of his interim test checks to include an enquiry into the allegations.
In order to facilitate this, the Board decided on February 22, 1965 to relieve the National Secretary of his duties (without loss of emolument) and to appoint an acting office manager for the period of one month required for the enquiry. Arrangements satisfactory to both parties were made during this time for the disposition of the National Secretary's personal effects and mail.
At a meeting of the Board held in Montreal on March 26, 1965, an interim report (pending completion of the audit of the Fund's operations for the full fiscal year which ended March 31, 1965) from the Office of the Auditor General was received and examined. May 4, 1965

speechtext:
have pleasure in announcing the names of the members of the Special Committee on Corrections which was forecast some time ago and mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. The composition of the Committee is as follows: Chairman, Hon. Mr. Justice Roger Ouimet, of the Superior Court of the Province of Quebec, District of Montreal; Vice Chairman, Mr. G. Arthur Martin, Q.C., Toronto. The two other members are Mrs. Dorthey McArton, B.A., of Winnipeg and Mr. W T McGrath, B.A., M.S.W., of Ottawa.
Mr. Justice Ouimet has long taken a keen interest in the field of corrections. Mr. Martin is a very well known defence lawyer. We have made no representations to the United States with respect to the position of ex-President Bosch in this matter, or what should be his position in developments as they occur within the Dominican Republic. Naturally-and I do not think it is necessary for us to tell the United States Government this-we hope that any political arrangements which are made for the restoration of peace and security to the island will be made by and for the people of the Dominican Republic.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASED STAFF IN OFFICES ABROAD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. In view of the fact that the large number of applications from the Portugese community of Waterloo South for the admission of relatives to Canada has seriously overloaded the facilities of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and is causing long delays in the processing of these applications, can the Minister inform the House if it is his intention to increase staff so these requests may be handled promptly?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASED STAFF IN OFFICES ABROAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the simple answer to the question is yes, but I feel that some further explanation is called for. Consideration is being given to increases in the staffs of several of our immigration offices in western and southern Europe, and to the establishment of some additional offices. In saying this I wish to make it clear that I am not referring specifically to our office in Portugal but rather to Europe generally.
I am sure the hon. Member and other hon. Members will appreciate that when we were faced with the serious unemployment situation that existed in Canada up until a relatively short time ago, the extent to which we should step up our immigration services was questionable, especially in those countries from which we were getting immigrants, having no special skills or trades. I might say that the situation is very different today, and the Assistant Deputy Minister of Immigration and the Director of Overseas Immigration Services have been in western Europe for about 10 days, I believe, visiting the different offices. My Deputy Minister and the Director of Immigration Services here in Canada are joining them later this week for a full scale discussion in London, and inquiry as to what additional staff and what additional facilities may be needed.
May 4. 1965

Inquiries of the Ministry [DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I might say that the prime purpose or prime objective of this meeting is the accumulation of information that is needed for the white paper upon which we are now working. The information is required largely because of discussions we have had with several of the Provinces, some four or five at least, and with industry regarding the need for skilled workers. The whole matter is under active study.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED SHORTAGE OF FRONT LINE INFANTRY BATTALIONS
speechtext:
My question is for the Minister of National Defence, and it is based on an article in last Saturday's Ottawa Journal which reads in part as follows:
The Canadian Army is so hard pressed for infantry battalions that the defence department has had to select for U.N. duty in Cyprus, the unit which performs the changing of the guard ceremony on Parliament hill.
I wonder if the Minister could tell the House whether or not there is a shortage of front line infantry battalions in the country at the present time, and what steps are being taken to bring the second battalion Canadian Guards up to full strength.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REPORTED SHORTAGE OF FRONT LINE INFANTRY BATTALIONS
speechtext:
There is no shortage of battalions. The number of battalions has been fixed for a considerable period of time. As I indicated last year, the changing of the guard on Parliament Hill does interfere with the training requirements of the Guards battalions. Nevertheless, it was considered advisable to continue this national ceremony this summer. I am sure we will be able to make up the deficit from the other battalions in order to enable both battalions to do their work during the summer.



May 4, 1965

speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Labour whether he feels he will be able, at an early date, to make a statement to the House about what changes in the administration and program of the National Employment Service have taken place since it was transferred to the jurisdiction of his department. subtopic: CHANGES NECESSITATED BY TRANSFER OF JURISDICTION
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the National Employment Service is now part of the Department of Labour. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is certainly a wait and see budget. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) delivered his budget address the other night it was well nigh impossible to count the number of times he used the expression, "we shall have to wait and see", or something similar to it.
Members of this House and the Canadian people must fully recognize that Canada's financial position is strengthened and our economy moves forward only when the Government does everything possible to improve and strengthen Federal-Provincial relations. Yet we are told to wait and see regarding Federal-Provincial relations and affairs relating to our constitution; wait and see while the Government stumbles from crisis to crisis; wait and see while the Government stumbles from crisis to crisis when basic action is needed immediately.
I say, together with the right hon. leader of my party, that the Government must immediately convene a national conference to study our constitution, and an all-party Parliamentary Committee should meet with similar bodies in every Province. The result will be a Made in Canada Constitution, a modern Constitution suited to modern times.

That conference must be convened as soon as possible. The Canadian constitution must be brought up to date; we need a constitution made right here in Canada.

We are asked to see whether the war on poverty will begin by itself. While those in the higher income brackets are to get a $600 tax saving, those in the lower brackets are to get a cut amounting to less than two cups of coffee a week. A Government which ignores the problems of price stability tells us to wait and see whether inflation will merely pass away. Meanwhile those who are trapped in grinding poverty must pay higher prices on fixed or shrinking incomes.
This Minister tells us to wait and see whether the war on poverty will begin by itself. We are told to wait and see whether by some stroke of magic the poor will become richer. Mr. Speaker, the budget is meant to be the Government's main annual social and economic document outlining, together with its course of action, the objectives of the administration both short term and long term.
I ask the Minister: Is this the beginning of the war on poverty, or does the Government merely intend to raise the expectations of

May 4, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Grafftey Canadians living in poverty and want by cruel and empty slogans, although it is action which is needed, and needed now?
The young people and the students of Canada are told to wait and see by a Government which hopes they will conveniently forget the promise of 10,000 university scholarships; by a Government which attempts to mobilize the idealism of youth while turning its back on its election speeches and promises. A Government which tolerates wrongdoing in high places and permits at least three and possibly four or five of its Members and supporters to remain in this House, when in any other free Parliament in the Western world those Members would long since have departed. Hon. gentlemen opposite wait and see and hope the public will conveniently forget that complete integrity is a prerequisite of good government in Canada.
We have to wait and see whether our products can become competitive at home and abroad while a tax of 11 per cent is hung around the necks of many of our producers. The farmer is told to wait and see by a confused Minister of Agriculture who keeps telling eastern farmers they never had it so good. Well, last Sunday a farmer phoned me in my riding and said: "In 1958 I received $3.10 per hundred for my milk and I am still receiving $3.10 per hundred for my milk". I should like the Minister to repeat to that farmer his statement that "he never had it so good". I will tell you one thing, Mr. Speaker. The poor farmers in Eastern Canada will not wait for the war on poverty to begin while the Minister responsible for rural development forgets the job he should really be doing and goes around wondering whether the new wing of the Liberal Party is going to survive in Quebec. The public in general, finding it difficult to afford the high cost of drugs and medicines, is told to wait until the Minister is given the findings of a committee report. I will say this: No Minister of Finance in the history of this young country has waited for the findings contained in so many reports, while an angry public witnessing the breaking of one promise after another calls for action. Management and labour are told to wait and see by a Minister of Finance who refuses to chart short and long term goals. At the same time, the majority of the recommendations of the Economic Council are either ignored, misunderstood, or, what is even worse, put on the shelf. Businessmen want to know more about the Canada Development

Plan before the private sector of the economy can raise investment capital. They, too, are told to wait by an indifferent Minister. The universities need help-not tomorrow but today. They, too, are told to wait and see, pending the report of the Bladen Commission. Hundreds of students were turned down by our medical schools this year. A lack of research and teaching facilities is the major reason for this state of affairs. Our medical schools are crying for increased assistance in research but they, too, are told to wait and see by an indifferent Government and by an indifferent Minister. Textile manufacturers are told to wait and see by a Government which will not or cannot arrive at sensible and realistic agreements with our trading partners.
Why is this a "Wait and See" budget? The answer should be very clear to most Members of this House. The fact is we are still suffering from the effects of the first budget which the Minister brought before this House. For the first time in the history of this country a Minister of Finance had to withdraw all the major proposals he had made. It was easily the worst budget ever presented in the history of Canada. The hon. gentleman had to withdraw all the major proposals of his first budget and he is now too terrified and too timid to act when action is patently necessary.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As he stands paralysed in a strait-jacket of fear an anxious Canadian public "waits and sees" how long the Prime Minister will allow him to occupy such a sensitive post in our nation.
I have already drawn attention in my opening remarks to the need for calling a national constitutional conference as soon as possible. We know that no plans which the Minister may make to better the financial and economic position of this country can come to fruition unless everything possible is done to improve our constitution and lead to better Federal-Provincial relations. But this Government-and I speak as a Canadian representing a riding made up for the greater part of the two founding races of this country -stupidly stumbles from crisis to crisis. The Minister of Finance is a prime example. His whole domestic economic program floundered on the rocks because he did not understand the basic initiatives required in the field of Federal-Provincial relations. He should have made himself familiar with this situation

years ago. But he failed to do so and as a result his whole program floundered with consequent damage to our national unity. Last week we saw a dispute between this Government and the Government of Quebec over treaty making powers. This week it is a dispute between this Government and the Province of Quebec over job placements. A new dispute has arisen over housing.
Why has this situation come about? It is because Members opposite refuse to heed in a bipartisan way the suggestions made by my right hon. leader-suggestions which were not made in a party spirit but for the good of Canada because in this instance, as in all other instances, the Leader of the Opposition places his country before party. This Government refuses to convene a national conference to renew and modernize our constitution. Its Members simply stumble from crisis to crisis.
Why must such a conference be held? This has been explained time and time again in the House but it must be repeated until this Government learns. Many metropolitan areas are today administering budgets larger than the budgets of some Provinces. These metropolitan areas are not cities and towns in the old 1867 sense. While they fall within the jurisdiction of the Provinces, which have the primary responsibility, the Federal Government certainly cannot turn its back on the many complex problems facing our sprawling city and metropolitan areas today. There is education, which falls under the purview of the Provincial Governments. Who in 1867 would have ever envisaged the expenditure on education which is taking place today?

This is another point I want to make, Mr. Speaker. It is hard to explain in words, but in many ways I have learned it since coming to this House of Commons and associating with many of my good colleagues from the West. What is going on in Quebec today? The Legislature of the Province of Quebec are studying necessary changes in our constitution; but I feel that very often we in the East fail to realize that since 1867 between the lakehead and the foothills of the Rockies, millions of Canadians have poured into the great West of our land. Today these people have a unique, outward-looking and dynamic idea of what Canada should be and should look like. Instead of dividing this country by inactivity, when will this Government accept the suggestion of our right hon. leader and do the basic job that is necessary?

The people from my Province perhaps have a different idea of what Canada should look like today than have the people in other parts of Canada. I happen to think that regionalism in many ways is a good thing as we underline "unity in diversity" in Canada today. But surely the time has come for these points of view to be brought to the conference table, instead of smearing my leader every time he opens his mouth about my Province. When he makes a suggestion to better Quebec, he is smeared with this anti-Quebec label. Every time he puts forward a suggestion inside or outside this House, he is smeared in this regard-and I know that the Liberals are up to their same old tricks-with "anti-Quebec", "anti-Canadian".

Last night Mr. Lesage came to Ottawa. Next week Mr. Pearson will go to Quebec City; and he gives throughout the country the impression that he is in the process of working out an agreement between two countries.
I ask the Prime Minister to convene such a national conference as soon as possible.

Sir, every day this Government waits to establish such a national conference to study our Constitution is a wasted day. The Canadian people will not tolerate this. They will not wait and see whether or not the Prime Minister is going to negotiate us out of Confederation. The Canadian people want to see the Prime Minister lead us into one united Canada. This suggestion will certainly have to be acted upon very, very soon, and the people of Canada will not wait and see.
What about the war on poverty. The Throne Speech said that the Government was going to declare a war on poverty.

speechtext: On the poor.

speechtext:
Again I say, Sir, that every sensible Member of this House and every conscientious Canadian recognized that if the Government was really sincere, it was in the budget, the major annual, social and economic document of the Government, that the government should outline in some detail at least how they would carry out this war on poverty. But what do we see? While those in the higher income brackets-I repeat again-are accorded a $600 tax reduction,
900	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Grafftey the lower income bracket earner gets a couple of cups of coffee a week. The question of inflation, which so touches the poor people in our country who are living in grinding poverty, was not considered by the Minister at all. The Minister falls into the classical pitfall of the affluent society. He has the gall to quote statistics to the millions of Canadians living in poverty, destitution or deprivation. It is not statistics they want from the Minister of Finance, who looks upon their plight with indifference, but they want action from a Government that is bogged down in the mire of indecision and confusion.
Mass poverty is one thing in the African and Asian countries. It is yet another thing in Canada where we have the second highest standard of living in the world. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure this is the opinion of many Members of this House, far too many Canadians are not truly sharing in our nation's prosperity. Right here, at home, we have done a poor job at pushing back the frontiers of poverty and want. Individual and national excellence will be a meaningless idea if millions of Canadians continue to barely exist in substandard conditions. We shall have to put an end to poverty in the midst of plenty at home, otherwise what will our answer to Communism be abroad? I will tell the Government this, Mr. Speaker, that you do not declare war on poverty in a concrete way by slogans alone.
The gross national product-and this is something the Minister of Finance should be very well aware of, and yet he is not, as he cites statistics and tells the people they have never had it so good-may be up and unemployment may be down; yet the poor still remain poor. In fact, very often an ever increasing gross national product locks more people into poverty. Today our rising gross national product means that many Canadians are becoming richer, while more than 4 million are becoming poorer. Four fifths of us earning salaries or having incomes tied to rising production or prices are not affected by this, but the other one fifth must pay these higher prices with shrinking and dwindling incomes. I ask myself, what percentage of this one fifth group will be covered by contemplated measures such as the Canada pension plan? I ask myself, what percentage of this one fifth group will be helped by this budget which is meant to begin the war on poverty-and I say none, Sir. I think it is a depressing thing when a Government, with slogans, builds up and raises the expectations

DEBATES	May 4, 1965
of millions of Canadians living in poverty and want, and the first major document, namely their budget, which they bring before this country has nothing in it for the poor.
Today rural poverty has become a great challenge to all of us. The rural poor and unemployed are to be found in our countryside, villages and small towns. A farmer owning his own land must gross $2,500 a year if he wishes to barely exist. By these standards we have subsisting at or under such a level 500,000 rural families. These families, together with the city poor, make up one fifth of our nation's population. The rural poor of this nation will not wait for the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development to decide, while he neglects his job, whether the new guard of the Liberal Party is going to survive in the Province of Quebec. Instead of the Minister continuing his war with the Prime Minister regarding who is going to clean out the old guard in Quebec, when is he going to administer his department and meet the challenge of rural poverty in this nation?
As the more affluent members of our society move to the suburbs, the city poor are still to be found in the millions at the centre of our metropolitan regions. Here we find the disabled, the unskilled and the aged in rundown housing areas. Need I say more in order to spell out the problem, Sir? Let us face it with the realization that wherever there is economic opportunity most men will willingly work. What are some first steps? Having found out where poverty is located, the next step involves the appropriate remedies. What are they? Roads, schools, parks and hospitals must be built by governments. And let us not imagine that only a small amount of money is involved in this regard. Area development, rehousing, retraining, health measures, urban renewal are only a few matters we should act upon immediately.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I should now like to deal with rural areas, Sir. First of all the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act legislation must be spurred on. Rural poverty has been largely located, and there is absolutely no excuse for further delays in implementing concrete plans which will bring results in terms of better land use, good farmers on good farms and social justice for those who wish to remain in rural areas.
Second, more vocational and trade schools must be built and staffed. As medium and light industries move into rural areas these schools will train and retrain rural citizens

who do not wish to locate and should not be relocated in our cities.
Third, straight grants to industries, for training or retraining workers up to definite standards on the job should be considered.
Mr. Speaker, when tax concessions are given to certain companies moving into designated areas, unemployment figures should not be the only statistics or factors considered before an area is so designated. Often there is no unemployment in a region simply because there is no growth. The grinding poverty and stagnation is appalling.
Let me refer to some first steps in respect of our cities and our metropolitan areas. While cities and towns come under the jurisdiction of the Provinces, many of our larger metropolitan areas are no longer cities in the sense they were in 1867. Today many metro governments administer larger annual budgets than a great number of our Provinces. While the Provinces have their primary responsibilities over cities and towns, the Federal Government cannot turn its back on the problems facing our sprawling cities and metropolitan areas.
Sir, in 1961 the Federal Government and Provinces called a conference relating to our material resources. The result was the eminently successful Resources for Tomorrow Conference. This was a high water mark in Federal-Provincial co-operation. In a similar spirit I believe that after much preparation the Federal Government and Provinces should call a conference on human capital and human resources.
To a great extent such a conference would involve problems facing our cities and metropolitan areas. Principles would be laid down and a line of action determined. Urban renewal, rehousing, communications, physical fitness, automation, delinquency, problems facing the aged and disabled, health and social justice would certainly head the list on the agenda of the conference.
These are merely some first steps that I believe must be taken immediately in order to face and solve a problem that has been with us far too long. The continuance of grinding poverty is not inevitable. If it is, what does democracy mean to the millions of Canadians who live in destitution, poverty or deprivation? This budget takes no first step in the war on poverty, and the time to begin is not tomorrow but now.
Sir, let us look at the economic goals for Canada to 1970 as outlined in the first annual report of the Economic Council of 22620-58

Let us look at three of the five goals stated in the Council's terms of reference. The first goal listed is that of "a reasonable stability of prices." In Canada last year over 3 per cent of our gross national productivity gain can be attributed to inflation and higher prices. Yet in his budget address the Minister ignored the problem as if it never existed. Certainly no constructive proposals were made in this regard. If the Minister continues to ignore this problem he does so at his own and certainly at his nation's peril.
The second goal listed by the Economic Council's annual report is "a viable balance of payments". In order to attain this goal I believe our products must remain competitive in the world markets, but the failure to abolish the 11 per cent tax, and the budget failure to advance one single measure to increase productivity brings us no closer to this goal.
The third goal set out by the annual report is an "equitable distribution of rising incomes." Mr. Speaker, I read this to mean that more Canadians should share in our nation's prosperity. Certainly more Canadians should share in our nation's prosperity, just as the Government should begin this war on poverty. A budget that favours the high income earner with a $600 per year tax saving and the lower income earner with a tax saving equivalent to the cost of a couple of cups of coffee, and a Government that ignores the effects of inflation on the 30 per cent of our population living in poverty, destitution, and deprivation, Sir, does not seem to be concerned very much with the goal of "an equitable distribution of rising income."
The first annual review of the Economic Council of Canada points out time and time again that Government has a major role to play in encouraging individual and national excellence. This budget now under discussion fails to recognize this fact.
Mr. Speaker, naturally every political party would claim to be the champion in encouraging individual and national excellence. This is to be expected. It is not my purpose to challenge other parties' views. I merely wish to underline what I consider the basic Conservative approach to the subject. While the Conservative recognizes that, in many ways, the old frontier days are a thing of the past, he still places great importance on the individual citizen and his legitimate aspirations. He also recognizes that nations are best at

The Budget-Mr. Lamontagne doing certain things. Nations, like individuals, have their specific aptitudes and qualities. In brief, the Conservative places a high premium on constructive national purpose and individual enterprise. This is no mere cliche, but something that is deeply felt and deeply believed in, namely that the Government has a dynamic role to play in encouraging individual and national excellence. That is something this Government has failed to recognize, but must begin to recognize if Canada is to move forward as a country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I should first like to draw the attention of the House to the new environment in which the budget has been brought down, and to which reference was made by the hon. Member immediately preceding me in the debate.
Since the last budget, we have had the first results of an exciting and significant experiment in national economic planning. I am referring to the first annual review of the Economic Council of Canada. This Council, which held its first meeting in January 1964, and published its first report in January 1965, is made up of three full time members-a chairman, a vice chairman and a director, who serve in their professional capacity as economists-and 25 part time members who were appointed after consultation with appropriate organizations. The latter were drawn approximately equally from four areas: labour, industry and commerce, agriculture and other primary industries, and the general public.
The Council has acquired a small but singularly competent staff of highly qualified experts. It is a unique organization, a sort of continuing royal commission on Canada's economic prospects and potential. Its first report provides, in my view, a strategy for policy, a set of goals and targets against which the actual performance of the economy should be measured. It provides a prescription of what the Canadian economy can and should achieve in the period to 1970. For the first time in the Canadian experience there exists the essential and basic framework within which economic planning in the public and private sectors can be effected. Within this framework the needs of tomorrow can be brought to bear on the policies of today.
This Government believes in economic planning, in indicative planning. We believe

that, in the face of a rapidly changing technological, commercial and political environment, a conscious and organized attempt must be made to co-ordinate public and private policies more rationally in order to reach agreed upon economic goals. This kind of planning should proceed in three stages. There should be an examination and specification of national goals in the light of the economy's potentialities and prospects. On the basis of a comprehensive assessment of the problems which may arise in achieving these goals, advice should be forthcoming on the means to achieve economic potentials. Policies, public and private, appropriate to bringing the prospects in line with the potentialities should be pursued and encouraged.
Within this framework of indicative planning the vital role which has been assigned to the Economic Council is to indicate the economic potentialities, to specify the national goals and targets, and to advise on the means to achieve them. The role of the budget and other Government policies is to use such advice to change economic prospects, if necessary, so that they will fulfil the potentialities. This is why from now on the budget ought to be considered and reviewed in the light of the annual reports of the Economic Council.
In its first annual review the Council dealt with the prospects and problems of the Canadian economy during the period to 1970. That report should carry great weight not only because of the excellence of its analytical content and substance but also because it is an expression of a consensus achieved amongst important decision makers in the private sector, including labour leaders, businessmen and representatives of the general public.
What are the goals and potentialities indicated by the Council? They are briefly defined as follows, and I will be more specific than the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). The first goal is a net increase of a million and a half jobs from 1963 to 1970; second, an average annual rate of increase of 5.5 per cent in total real output and, third, an annual rate of unemployment of 3 per cent. A necessary condition in achieving of these targets, according to the Council, is a reasonable degree of price and cost stability. The Council suggests that if the range of price and cost movements can be successfully contained within the limits of the relatively moderate average annual
May 4, 1965
changes in prices and costs annually recorded in Canada over the past decade, that is, 2 per cent, this necessary condition will have been met. In the opinion of the Council, if these targets are achieved we will have a high standard of living and a high employment economy in the period to 1970. If they are not achieved, then our economy will operate below its potential unless specific steps are taken to improve economic prospects. The Government, as indicated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), has accepted the targets and the goals proposed by the Economic Council.
It is in the light of these goals, therefore, that we must appraise the economic prospects for 1965 as indicated in the budget speech. What are the prospects? The Minister of Finance has stated that in the last two years 500,000 new jobs have been created in our country. This certainly reveals a healthy rate of improvement which, if sustained, will result in achieving the Council's employment target some time in 1968 instead of 1970. The Minister of Finance forecasts an increase in prices of goods and services within the range suggested by the Council. However, the prospective performance of the economy in 1965 falls short of the targets in two respects. The Minister of Finance forecasts an increase of 5 per cent in real output instead of the 5.5 per cent average proposed by the Council, and the most recent statistics reveal a rate of unemployment of 3.9 per cent of the labour force. Such conditions, in the Council's view, call for a relatively small deficit. Indeed, the members of the Council say:
"We would favour a combination of levels of tax rates and expenditure programs which would yield a rough balance if the economy were operating at potential output."
Since the economy in 1965 is expected to operate slightly below its potential, the Minister of Finance has decided to stimulate total demand, more specifically consumer demand, and to cut taxes in a way intended to close still further the gap between the level of performance of the economy and its potential rate of real output. This should help also further to reduce unemployment.
We are, therefore, rapidly approaching the stage where we will have eliminated what the Council has termed "demand deficient unemployment". This, however, is not sufficient. We all realize that we must address ourselves to the problem of hard core unemployment and that measures other than tax cuts are needed to alleviate structural 22620-58J
The Budget-Mr. Lamontagne or chronic unemployment. The Council in its report has a great deal to say about the need for upgrading the skills and enhancing the mobility of our labour force. The Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) is developing new manpower policies with the objective of achieving an optimum utilization of our rapidly growing labour force. This comprehensive program will attempt to remove the occupational, industrial and geographic obstacles that stand between the displaced worker and his new job. Better criteria are being developed to be applied to designated areas. Greater assistance through ARDA and the Department of Industry will be available to those areas where unemployment is high and where incomes, if they are available at all, are low. We intend to implement, in collaboration with the Provinces, new and better co-ordinated regional policies which will create new opportunities for depressed areas, and cure chronic pockets of unemployment in a way consistent with the achievement of the national economic goals.

The Council indicates that the effective achievement of potential output, with adequate accompanying labour market policies and other measures to facilitate adjustment to change, will significantly improve the standards of living of low income groups. However, the Council recognizes "that there will be Canadians who, for various reasons, will be unable to participate in the high employment and income opportunities under conditions of rapid and sustained growth and whose poverty may become more acute and more obvious in a high income, high growth economy". The war on poverty program announced by the Government is an energetic response to his challenge. The budget is the Government's first participation in the new Canadian experiment in planning.
In January the Economic Council provided the strategy for policy. It has indicated the targets, the goals and the potentialities of the Canadian economy through to 1970. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has presented policies which will contribute to our economy, realizing its potential in the participation of that strategy. This is a landmark in our history and the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated for having taken this very important step which places the budget in a completely new prospective.
We are also, of course, most grateful to the Economic Council for its very fine report. From now on, no serious economic discussion

May 4, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Lamontagne can take place without taking into consideration the work of this new and significant national institution. The Government, in the Budget, has accepted the goals and prescriptions of the Economic Council. Those who are opposed to the budget proposals should also, if they want to be consistent, attack the Council's report on which these proposals are based, and say how and why the targets and recommendations of the Council are deficient. The Members of the Opposition during this debate are not even trying to do so.

In his speech the Minister of Finance also dealt with the federal-provincial relations problem. I should also like to deal with it. I will first go over the main stages in the development of our political system since 1867; I will then explain the nature of cooperative federalism and, finally, show the main results obtained since its inception just two years ago.
From 1867 to 1920, the central government dominated within our confederation. The political union of 1867 was a compromise between legislative union and confederation. On the other hand, the federal government assumed the great tasks of the state, at the time, and provincial legislatures were put under its control. It was to organize the former colonies into a common market, standardize the currency, extend the territory from the Atlantic to the Pacific, help to develop the country by completing the railway and canal system, foster colonization through immigration and protect infant industries by establishing customs tariff. It was given full authority to discharge its duties in the fields of currency, national and international trade, and it could use every means or systems of taxation.
Such was the spirit of confederation in the beginning. Although the provinces gradually freed themselves, it is safe to say that this federalism, which I shall call a trusteeship federalism, was maintained until after the first world war.
The second important phase of our political evolution took place between 1920 and 1940 and was marked by provincial supremacy and by a federalism of coexistence. The federal government had accomplished the great tasks it had been entrusted with in 1867. On the other hand, due to technical progress -the invention of the automobile for instance-due to industrialization and urbanization, which also became sources of eco-

nomic instability and social insecurity, due finally to some decisions of the privy council, the field of provincial responsibilities was considerably widened in such areas as highways, education and welfare, because the municipalities could no longer cope with the task.
During that same period the provinces had to increase their revenues and instead of using the field of direct taxation which was opened to them, they invaded, through a legal stratagem, the field of indirect taxation which was prohibited to them under the constitution. In the province of Quebec, for instance, taxes on gasoline, which are indirect taxes, were levied as early as the 1920s, while the first provincial personal income tax which is a direct tax, was levied in 1939. Thus, during that period, every province widened the scope of its responsibilities and increased its sources of revenues without paying attention to the actions of the neighbouring provinces and of the federal government which was marking time anyhow. That was the era of coexisting federalism.
The depression of the thirties was to lead to the bankruptcy of that confederative federalism and the second world war was its finishing stroke. Confederative federalism had not solved the economic and social problems of that time but it had led several provinces to the threshold of bankruptcy.
The third phase of our political evolution, from 1940 to 1963, started with the second world war and was characterized by a return to central predominance. During the post-war period, when the hard times of the depression were still in everybody's mind and when the provinces did not have any inclination nor administrative capability to give leadership, the federal government assumed the new tasks of the welfare state in an attempt to deal with the problems that confederative federalism had not been able to settle. The tasks, briefly, were to promote industrial development, stabilize the economy at the level of full employment and set up a comprehensive system of social security. In order to carry on efficiently its new functions, the federal government thought it necessary to enjoy an exclusive use of direct taxation. That is why the wartime fiscal arrangements were extended, with some amendments. So the central government was, once again, in control of the economic and social activities of the country, acting alone or offering to share in joint plans with the provinces. We had thus come back to an inflexible trusteeship fed-
May 4, 1965
eralism wanted by the poorer provinces, tolerated by the rich provinces and where only Quebec was practising a passive opposition.
In my opinion, two very important lessons arise from our political experience and that of other countries having a federal constitution. The first concerns the distribution of functions between the various spheres of government. Not only is it desirable but it is also necessary for the sake of order to assign certain duties exclusively to one government or the other; however, it is impossible to set up a definite and comprehensive system of distribution of government responsibilities in a complex and changing society.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Federalism has to be adjusted constantly as the duties of the state change and its responsibilities increase. Every time such changes occur, the necessity arises of redistributing the duties between the different levels of government. Consequently, federalism is never definitely settled.
A tight partitioning of the duties of the state is also impossible. The existence of men living in society constitutes a well-integrated entity; we can, to be sure, make distinctions between various areas in the abstract and consider them separately, but realities do not permit such distinctions. Human problems, whether economic, social or cultural, are becoming increasingly indivisible and their necessary solutions are often beyond the limits set up at first.
There will always be matters of concurrent jurisdiction and problems, such as unemployment, which will require joint action by the governments in order to be solved in the best way possible. In other words, governments, within federalism, can rightly consider themselves as independent from one another in some fields, but in many others, they must consider themselves as interdependent, if they are fully aware of their responsibilities with regard to the common good of their citizens.
The second lesson emerging from our political evolution is that interdependence, however essential to federalism, has never been recognized until lately through a system of consultation and co-ordination of government policies. That is why in a great measure, our federalism has swayed from one extreme to the other, from a trusteeship system to a quasi-confederative system-an extreme gradually generating its opposite-without ever striking a happy medium.
The Budget-Mr. Lamontagne
It is precisely that middle point, that happy medium between trusteeship federalism and confederative federalism which is struck by co-operative federalism. This type of federalism could be summarized in three words: interdependence, consultation and coordination in fields of concurrent jurisdiction or in matters requiring joint action on the part of the governments.
The era of co-operative federalism was born in 1963. Since July of that year, five plenary federal-provincial conferences and several other special meetings were held. During that time, there have been nearly constant contacts between senior officials of both levels of government.
At the Quebec conference, it was decided to set up a federal-provincial tax structure committee. Composed of cabinet ministers and experts, the committee has been entrusted with the task of suggesting, on the basis of new government priorities, new ways of sharing the taxation fields. We have here a collective study that could very well lead us to entirely new approaches in a vital area of our federalism.
During the past two years, the organization of the Montreal world fair and the confederation centennial has been modified to ensure the full co-operation of all governments. The federal government's municipal loan fund has been established without infringing on provincial jurisdiction over local authorities. Finally, a contributory old age pension plan was set up with the best features of both the initial federal scheme and the Quebec program for the greatest benefit of all Canadians. There you have, in short, the first results of co-operative federalism.
Even if, essentially, co-operative federalism boils down to the idea of interdependence, consultation and co-ordination of some important government policies, it also has other characteristics. For instance, co-operative federalism must be associated with the idea of decentralization, in the present circumstances.
The provincial governments have considerably improved their civil service in the last few years; therefore, they are in a better position than ever before to face their own responsibilities. Besides, their will to assume those responsibilities themselves is stronger. From that standpoint, Quebec does not go against the general trend but is leading the movement. Finally, it could not be denied, two years ago, that the provinces had to get more revenues and that some of their responsibilities had priority.

May 4, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Lamontagne
Because of those various factors, and others as well, trusteeship federalism is a thing of the past and co-operative federalism, based on consultation and co-ordination between equals, would be impossible without decentralization. That is at least a concomitant to the establishment of a new federalism. What have we done in that regard in the last two years?
First, we have promoted justice and fiscal decentralization. As early as November 1963, by re-establishing the principle of equalization, we have repaired the injustice done to Quebec and to other provinces, as compared with Ontario, in 1962. Besides, the exclusive share of succession duties coming to the provinces has been increased from 50 to 75 per cent. Under a commitment made in April 1964, the provincial share of the personal income tax will be increased by 2 per cent in 1965-66 and by another 2 per cent in 1966-67. Finally, we gave another 3 per cent to Quebec to make up for the extension of family allowances, which had already been done in that province.
What do all those changes mean in additional revenue for Quebec in particular? If you take into account the extension of the technical training program, our province will receive approximately $300 million more, from 1964 to 1967, under the new federal-provincial arrangements made in the last two years.
We promoted fiscal and legislative decentralization in another important way. We gave the provinces the opportunity to opt out of joint programs already existing and entailing relatively stable annual expenditures and offered to compensate the provincial governments by increasing their share of direct taxes and equalization payments. That reform, approved in its first stage by parliament recently, will give a new direction to our federalism, will center it more strongly on provincial autonomy and will enable the provinces to assume their own responsibilities if they so desire.
The federal contribution to joint programs covered by the opting out formula amounted to approximately $644 million in 1963-64.
The province of Quebec, by taking advantage of this offer, will receive by way of compensation, besides deficiency and equalization payments, 20 per cent of the federal personal Income tax in the form of an exclusive and additional taxation right.
That is an unprecedented measure of decentralization in our political history. Early in 1962, the portion of federal personal in-

come tax that Quebec could collect while still avoiding double taxation was 13 per cent. In 1966-67, if we take into consideration the new fiscal arrangements and the implementation of the opting out formula, that portion will reach 47 per cent. With the equalization payments, it will go over 70 per cent.
With trusteeship federalism, the strength of the central government rested too often on the weakness of the provinces. With con-federative federalism, the strength of the provinces rested on the weakness of the federal government.
I think we should avoid those two extremes which were detrimental to the interests of the Canadian people in the past. The decentralization movement which was initiated in 1963 is a sound one, for it announces the end of the trusteeship federalism. However, the new growing strength of the provinces should not rest on the weakness of the central government in its own fields of jurisdiction. Such an outcome would not be in the interests of Canadians who would sooner or later ask for a return to trusteeship federalism. A strong and prosperous Quebec more particularly needs a powerful and dynamic Canada.
That is why since 1963, the federal government has taken again the initiative at the international level and considerably increased our assistance to underdeveloped countries. We have put the monetary, trade and fiscal policies at the service of our industrial development, and, as a result, the Canadian economy presently enjoys a great development and unemployment has never been as low since 1957.
Finally, we are taking the necessary steps to strengthen the cultural institutions under our jurisdiction. As the chief editor of Le Devoir wrote on June 16, 1964:
We want a federal state strong and articulate enough to ensure efficiency in our country.
And I would add: so that it may play its part fully and vigorously in our political system.
Co-operative federalism, which strikes a happy medium between trusteeship federalism and confederative federalism, is rejected by both extremes facing each other at present in this country, by both separatisms, English and French. But I am sure it will be accepted by all Canadians endowed with clearsightedness and good will, who are the vast majority in this country, and that it will contribute to rebuild our national unity on a more realistic and more dynamic basis.
May 4, 1965

As bees on flowers alighting cease their hum, So settling on high places, Whigs grow dumb.

[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
What are the results of this indiscriminate, thoughtless way we have gone about our business over the years? We find that some of our biggest problems today are the water table levels in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Basin; flood damage across the country; the erosion of valuable, irreplaceable land; pollution of lakes and rivers; slums


in our cities and towns; sprawling suburbs on the outside of every city, completely cutting off recreational grounds and parklands from our citizens. Here we are with a brand new country to develop, and already we have our hands tied behind our backs because we are using half of our strength and wealth and everything else trying to correct the mistakes of the past, without being able to tackle the future.
How much of our energy and wealth today goes into trying to correct these ills of the past? Let us take a look at them. The Department of Forestry was brought into being for practically this sole purpose, because Governments of the past have permitted individuals and corporations to milk millions of dollars from our forest resources, leaving utter desolation behind them; and now we have to go back and pick up the pieces. This was followed, of course, in many areas by attempts to farm improper farmland that could never sustain farming. So we are met with pockets of poverty and degradation that we are going to have to cope with sooner or later. We have seen this put off and put off until finally it has got to the stage where it can be put off no longer. Our Department of Industry was instituted for practically the same purpose, to try and do something with the slow growth areas that are, again, a heritage of our past. The Department of Labour is trying desperately to cope with a situation where we have people flooding the labour market who have neither the education nor the skills to be absorbed back in industry. They are going to try and do something about that, again. There is the Department of Welfare, where so many of our older citizens and some of the more unfortunate ones have to trust themselves to the mercy of the various Governmental agencies that look after this sort of thing, or service clubs or the host of other bodies that are scratching around trying to do a job and not really accomplishing much.
How many Elliot Lakes have we got across this country, where millions and millions of dollars were squandered on a five-year contract, where people were enticed by the thousands to come in, and lost their homes and their life savings, while the companies and the industry were guaranteed their profit within the terms of that five-year contract? Now the latest word we have in the North Country is that to try and correct the mistakes of the past the Government are even going to try and steal the smelters, which

should properly go into the Timmins region, and put them into Elliot Lake to cover up for their past mistakes.
At the rate we are going it will only be a very short time before our whole budget will be required to try and correct the mistakes of the past. Right now we have to run like hell to stand still; and pretty soon, no matter how fast we run, we will be slipping back. And all because the growth and conservation and everything else was left in the past to the whim of individuals and the corporations whose only responsibility was to themselves and their shareholders, while the Government, which is supposed to bear the responsibility of the public and the country, have been taking this wealth that belonged originally to the people and have permitted individuals to make great fortunes out of it, leaving desolation behind them, and then calling on the people again to pick up the pieces and try and patch things up. This is the result we have after 97 years of Liberal and Conservative Government. This is the heritage we are faced with today. Each in its turn has evaded this responsibility to the country and the people of the country. Each of them has sounded very progressive w'hen in opposition. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a good idea for the people of Canda, before it is too late, would be to put them both in opposition, and when they both become progressive at the same time there might be some hope for this country in the future.
The Provinces today are showing far more leadership in this field than is our Federal Government. That is why today when you see agreements signed between the Federal Government and various Provinces you usually find they are what might be termed mutual agreements, with the Federal Government playing the part of a mute.

I am afraid that I only have a few moments left at my disposal, but I will be prepared to answer your question after I have completed my remarks.
We must realize that if we are going to do a job of this kind we must change our ideas. We must change our policies, such as the policy which has been in existence for some time in this country in respect of transportation. In this regard the taxpayer reaches in one pocket to subsidize the transportation of raw material, and in the other pocket to pay a superficially high price for the finished product. In other words, the taxpayer is paying to ship the raw material out, and paying to bring the finished product back in.
Such a policy may work satisfactorily in isolated areas where there is only a small amount of raw material which would not ordinarily be developed without the benefit of a transportation subsidization. At the present time such a suggestion in respect of the resources in the Timmins area would be considered as idiotic. No one would contemplate that it would be more economical to ship out that raw material by rail or by road, in spite of the transportation policy in this country.
Let me make it perfectly clear that I am not advocating that the companies that make these discoveries in our country should be throttled. We should recognize the principle that these companies should be allowed to
May 4, 1965

recover their exploration costs. They should also be permitted to make a reasonable and good profit. It should also be apparent to them, however, that the policy of this country is that these discovered resources must be developed in the best interests of the citizens of the discovery area, and of the country in which they have been found.
The Government must provide leadership in this regard. There is nothing whatever in this budget which gives me any encouragement that the Government has considered this idea, or realized the benefits of it and is prepared to carry it out. In fact, in view of all the economic circumstances which now exist in this country, it is my opinion that a Government which brings in this kind of budget at this time in this country should hang its head in shame.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my participation in this debate by complimenting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) upon his remarkable achievements over the past few years. Since he became the Minister of Finance he has managed to balance the nation's financial budget. He has changed the financial picture from a deficit of as high as 10 per cent to a balanced account. Shortly before he assumed his portfolio the Government was spending $110 for every $100 it was receiving, but during the past year he has been able to bring this situation close to the balancing point. If one is at all optimistic about the next year, more optimistic than the Minister of Finance was in his tentative forecast, he will also see a balanced budget for 1965.
It is not my intention to deal with the subject of a balanced budget because that is a secondary consideration. A balanced budget gives confidence to the business community and in respect of our international monetary affairs, but it is secondary to our over-all economic growth.
Unemployment during the last two-year period has been cut in half. That in itself is a remarkable achievement and one which is even more important than the balancing of a budget. Also in terms of our economy we have seen a remarkable rate of economic growth. There was an increase of something of the order of 2 per cent a year in the late 1950's and early 1960's, one which barely kept up with population growth. This rate of growth has been increased to approximately 6 per cent per annum. This is the kind of growth rate that we should maintain.
The Economic Council of Canada has indicated the desirability of maintaining a growth rate over a long period of something of the order of 5J per cent, in order to maintain an increase in labour demand which will accommodate the young citizens of this country who come of age and require jobs. This is something which must be considered in assessing the longer term factors influencing economic growth.
912	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Davis
During the remaining time available to me this afternoon I should like to direct my remarks toward the longer term outlook, and to concentrate particularly on scientific research and development. The scientist in his laboratory looks ahead for a great many years. He cannot expect the result of his efforts to be of any significant financial advantage to his employer within months, or even years. In other words, the investment in his time, and the plant and equipment he uses is predicated upon longer term expectations.
In this country we must specialize because of the relatively small size of our population and because, at least for the time being, of the relatively specialized nature of our industry. In the area of scientific research and development we should specialize as well.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In the current budget, there are measures of tax relief which will apply generally throughout our economy. These are measures which have the character, if I may use the phrase, of a shotgun approach to the stimulation of research and development. That is part of the necessary arsenal, but I also believe we need a few rifles as well. We need a specific approach to complement the shotgun approach of general tax concessions for research and development. In other words, we must also specialize in respect of Government support for research and development.
It used to be loosely said that the main factors promoting growth were land, labour and capital. By "land" was meant those resources which went along with the effort or musclepower of mankind and money. But today most economists agree that what is needed is more than that. We need resources, labour, although admittedly small amounts, and capital or money, but basically we also need ideas. Ideas are the fourth major element of economic growth. Indeed, ideas in the sense of research and development, the stimulation of new ideas and the production of new products and the creation of new and more efficient processes, are more important than man's physical effort. They are beginning to be regarded as more important than new capital in the sense of machinery and equipment. They are beginning to challenge even our basic resources such as forests, minerals, land and so on as the most important factor generating long term economic growth. So I should like to suggest that the industry of ideas is perhaps more important to us than any factor of production in this country, other than the raw resources. Indeed 
DEBATES	May 4, 1965
it is challenging the value of the resources themselves.
We in this country have very few people and consequently we have to try to magnify their importance by generating more ideas and easing the flow of ideas between ourselves, between corporations, between Government and industry in this country. This must be done to increase our long-term rate of economic growth, to make it of the order and magnitude which has been anticipated and set as a target by the Economic Council of Canada.
In addition to the flow of ideas I should like to stress the need to direct this effort in producing more ideas. I have suggested it should be directed in a more specialized fashion, perhaps in some cases toward resource development, certainly toward development in industries which have already shown some indication of success. In other words, we should reinforce success. The Government, as does private enterprise, should consciously direct its research effort more toward those activities in which we have already been successful in the hope and, indeed, the expectation that we will be more productive with the passage of time. We must manage these research and development activities.
One of the great problems in respect of research and development is compartmental-ization. A scientist shuts himself off in a laboratory and he stays to himself. He may generate ideas. He may even communicate with other scientists at great distances and they may have what they regard as a useful exchange of information. But this does not necessarily benefit those around them, certainly those engaged in the production of useful goods and services in their immediate vicinity. We need more communication between the scientist and the development engineer, and between them in turn and those responsible for production. There should also be more communication with those responsible for selling the product and those involved in financing, in getting costs and prices down and expanding output. In other words, the problem common to management of large corporations, of communication between basic research on the one side and increased sales and profitability on the other, must be met. We must try to do this in Canada. We must try to do it in an over-all sense. We must also break down the very obvious and, I think, flagrant compartmental-ization between Government and industry in this country.
May 4. 1965

Much of the research that has been done in Canada has been useful but it has been of the nature of basic or fundamental research. We in this country have specialized much more in basic and fundamental research than is the rule in more industrialized countries, certainly industrialized countries like the United Kingdom, West Germany and even the United States. They have applied the results of basic research but we have not been able to do so to the same extent.
Of our Federal outlays more than 80 per cent go into Government establishments of one kind or another. These Government establishments are rarely in direct communication either with our universities or with industry. It is because of this preponderance of effort in Government establishments, in what are usually called "in house" activities, departmental activities, N.R.C. activities and so on, and the lack of effort and the lack of financial assistance flowing from Government to industry and to the universities for research purposes, that we have failed to distinguish ourselves in the field of applied research-particularly in those fields which would inevitably result in a higher rate of economic growth.
This can be shown in reverse. I think one could even expand it into a tangible recommendation for a research policy. One need only look at the geographical development of research and development activities in a large country like the United States to indicate what should be done. In the most successful research and development complexes you need a university, preferably more than one; you need a government research establishment, preferably several in close proximity to the universities; and you certainly need science based on research and development conscious industries in close proximity to the universities and government research establishments.
There is one such complex in the Boston area. This is the most desirable type of development with universities, government research establishments and research conscious industries all in close geographical proximity one to the other.
Next in line, but less likely to spin off new products, are centres like Ann Arbor, in Michigan, where you have a university or universities and research conscious firms in close alliance with the graduate study departments and faculties of those universities. There are other developments in other places where government research laboratories of
The Budget-Mr. Davis quality have been established in close contact with industry, but for the greatest likelihood of success you need all three. You need universities, government research establishments and industries exchanging ideas one with the other.
In Washington, D.C., there are government laboratories and defence based industries. In Ottawa, Canada, as the result of large Federal investment in laboratories in this city we are beginning to see some science based industries. Those in the electronics field are good examples.
So far as Canada is concerned, as well as following the shotgun approach of tax concessions and grants generally to all industry in respect of research and development, I think we have to decide to promote centres of excellence, similar centres of intensive research and development activity in Canada. At the outset there will not be a very great number. We only have one or two at the present time. We also have to decide how we will specialize in each of them, perhaps a complex with emphasis on forest products research and development in one area, mineral processing in another, oceanography in a third, agriculture in a fourth, medicine in another, and so on.
This specialization is necessary because of our relatively small population and our limited financial resources. It is also necessary because of the basic economics of communication. Ideas which are generated in the universities, in the government laboratories, and in energetic firms with regard to new product development must be kicked around frequently. The opportunity to discuss them and take advantage of the most profitable must be present. It will only come about as the result of winnowing through innumerable ideas and inventions, many of which will never be productive in the commercial sense of the word.
I should like to say a little bit about management in research. Research is like everything else. It costs money and a vested interest arises in continuing that research. Personnel become wedded to the idea that some development will eventually materialize, regardless of the lack of current success. It is, therefore, necessary to bring some of these efforts to an end. Certainly, after five or ten years of frustrated effort other projects should be put in their place.
[DOT] (5:20 pjn.)
There are techniques being developed, certainly in private enterprise, for determining when ideas should be pursued, how long they

May 4, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Davis should be pursued, when they must be cut off by drastic surgery if necessary and when other more productive research undertaken. One type of analysis referred to generally by economists as benefit-cost analysis is sometimes applied. Simplified, it may be put in these terms: What is the hoped for benefit? This might be put down in one column in financial terms, that is the benefits listed out over the years. In another column, you list the annual costs. If total benefits exceed total costs, it is conceivable that you go ahead with the project. However, the benefits must exceed the costs in a ratio which reflects the probability of this experiment coming off. Indeed regard must be had continuously to the possibility of this particular research and development paying its way and, as an alternative, the possibility of paying royalties and getting others to supply the knowledge or know-how must always be kept in mind.
Canada has grown largely as a result of technological developments in other parts of the world, and our willingness to import these ideas and put them to work in a practical way in this country. I hope we will continue to do this, and continue to do it on the largest possible scale. So, in respect of our own research and development efforts, we must frequently look over our shoulder and consider the possibility of paying royalties to others to supply this technical knowhow rather than paying the cost of our own developments. A decision must be made based on the intimate knowledge of the prospects that are immediately before us. These checks and balances, therefore, should exist. Indeed they must exist in respect of our more massive Federal Government programs. I would suggest that this approach be applied soon to atomic energy in this country. We should take a good, hard look at a program which requires $50 million a year from the Canadian taxpayers, more than $2 per capita, more than $6 per family per year, which is a big investment in research and development in any enterprise. This is big league, to say the least. It is an enterprise in which other more financially competent countries, are engaged. It is this type of analysis which we must apply, not only toward big programs but lesser programs. This is the type of analysis which private business must apply in respect of research and development. I suggest more of this hard-headed type of approach should be applied to government research and development, and if it is it will release more money

for Canadian development in the years ahead.
I want to say a brief word about the new Science Council of Canada. We have, if we are following my reasoning, to pinpoint some of these major areas of development and not simply rely on the general tax incentives. We need advice here. I say "we" and I mean both Canadian industry and the Canadian Government. We need to have at the Government's elbow, and periodically releasing reports, an advisory committee like the Economic Council. And our Science Council should be made up not only of representatives of Government, but even more important, knowledgeable people in research and development from universities and from business.
