speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We should also decide which should receive assistance from Provincial Governments because we have in this country the problem of compartmentalization and a lack of communication between our several levels of Government as well. I trust that the new Science Council of Canada will perform these functions.
We already have in being a Science Secretariat, and that Secretariat will be the Secretariat for this Advisory Council. This Secretariat will work in close concert not only with the Economic Council in respect of economic judgments governing scientific endeavours, but also with Treasury Board in respect of other priorities.
Within Government each department, in my view, should have its own scientific group. This is particularly necessary in areas like Agriculture, Mines and Technical Surveys, Forestry, Fisheries and so on. This is not altogether agreed upon in other countries. In the United Kingdom at the moment they are withdrawing what technically I might
May 4, 1965



call scientific divisions or groups from other departments, and putting them into two newly established departments.
There has been recently constituted a new department of education and science and a new department of technology. The basic research activities and information activities go to the department of education and science. All other technical research and development go to the department of technology. In my view, this is a retrograde step. I think that scientists who are specialists in agriculture should be in the Department of Agriculture. I think scientists, like economists, should be distributed amongst the departments. Those who specialize should make their specialized knowledge available to the departmental officials responsible for administration and policy. Each Minister, in turn, will be better advised from a purely scientific point of view.
This raises the awkward question of coordination. It raises the awkward question of priorities. This is where the new Science Secretariat, advising the Science Council, can make its major contribution. It is interesting to note that in the United States, particularly since the late President Kennedy's election as President, there has been a science advisory council established there. Indeed, it is loosely referred to in Washington as the "inner sanctum for science". The President's scientific adviser is very close to the President. He has a small staff of 19 members. These men are men of broad experience, not necessarily scientists and certainly not practising scientists, but men with a general understanding of the usefulness of science. These men each cover broad general areas. In respect of water resource development, for instance, there is one man who looks at all scientific matters relating to water. He draws information from a great many departments-agriculture, the interior, the United States Corps of Army Engineers which is responsible for flood control, navigation and so on. This information is co-ordinated and priorities are established. They are established, first, with regard to the technical possibilities by this science secretariat and the last judgment is made by the bureau of the budget which, after getting advice from this scientific advisor decides which of these research and development activities shall proceed and which shall not.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I think in Canada the time has long since passed when we could do without a Science Council. We have had councils of different
The Budget-Mr. Davis types allied with the National Research Council. Initially they were set up to take a broad look, not only at Government activity but at research activity in industry as well. But they have tended to focus onto basic research, and in particular the activities of the National Research Council. They have not performed the function of co-ordinating and setting priorities, which the new Science Council will be asked to do.
It will use this permanent Science Secretariat which is being built up at the present time. This will be its staff, and the Science Secretariat at the same time will on occasion be the science staff for the Economic Council, and more particularly for the budget making officers in the Canadian Government.
I have referred very briefly to the organization of scientific matters in the United Kingdom and in the United States. In Sweden there is one central advisory council. The Prime Minister is the honorary Chairman of that council. This indicates that country's determination to make science and technology a subject of intimate knowledge to the top political level there. This has been eminently successful, and it parallels the recent United States practice.
It is at variance, however, with the current practice in the United Kingdom where basic science is being compressed into one department, technology into another department, and all other departments are left high and dry so far as an intimate knowledge of scientific affairs is concerned. I think Canada must avoid such a course.
Again I stress the need for communications. This is basically the industry of ideas. These ideas have to flow between people in different activities, in research, industry, sales and finance. They have to flow between governments and different levels of government, and hence communications are very important.
We need direction in the sense of specialization, particularly in a country like Canada, with a limited population and limited financial resources. We need specialization, not only backing up our more successful and profitable resource industries, but those of our industries which, because of tax and other assistance, show success. We need specialization in areas of development such as this which, because they have shown we can break through and lead the pack for the time being, can stand further encouragement and provide more income and employment for this country.

May 4, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Davis
As to the particular Minister to whom the Science Council should report, I am not so certain. It could report for the time being to the Prime Minister. It could report to the President of the Treasury Board, as recommended by the Glassco Commission. But this Science Council must certainly have a loud voice in Cabinet. It should have through that Minister, whether he be the Prime Minister or one of the other Ministers, a Minister who in effect acts as a sort of spark plug not only with the Government but in setting policy with respect to research and development in industry as well.
In this country, and indeed throughout the world, we are seeing time being compressed and space being compressed. We are seeing the industry of ideas growing at a rapid rate. Research and development is growing at an annual rate of 10 per cent in the United States. In this country we will do well to keep our expenditures on research and development rising at that rate. We must not emphasize, however, too much of the Government approach.
We need more activity in industry, in the applied fields, and particularly in universities, and it is in these second and third areas we need the greatest effort. There the annual growth rate in respect of research and development must be more like 25 per cent. This is the figure to which the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) referred recently, in respect to hoped for private industry investment in research and development-25 per cent. These, then, are some of the targets.
I compliment the Minister of Finance upon his general approach in respect to tax measures designed to encourage more research and development. This is the broad shotgun approach. But we still need decisions which focus upon specific industries, specific areas, and specific products. This more specialized approach, this rifle aiming approach, will be necessary in order to supplement our great effort in research and development.
In other words, I have been advocating a two pronged approach to research and development. If we take this course, and the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry and the Ministers responsible for all our other resource industry departments cooperate, we will achieve some of the economic targets which the Economic Council sets out for us in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, many things have been said about the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), some complimentary, others not. I would like to compliment him in one field in that he has driven more of his colleagues to the path of classical quotations and allusions than any other Member of the House. I have heard many people quoting the expression that the mountain was in labour and brought forth a mouse. I notice the hon. Member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) used a version of it from Horace last night.
Following in that vein I went back to read Phaedrus, and his version was as follows, "The mountain was in labour sending forth dreadful groans and there was the highest expectation throughout the region, but it brought forth only a mouse."
I recall the speculation in the press about what was going to happen, and comparing it with the reality I can understand why our colleagues headed in this direction. I found nothing in this afternoon's discussion from the opposite side which would lend support to the view maintained by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) that this document would make a good election budget. I
[Mr. Davis.)
May 4, 1965

do not know if he is unique in that point of view, or whether this is one of the times when it is not popular in that quarter of the House to suggest elections-this prompts me to recall another allusion to another great classical day, the time Horatius maintained the watch on the bridge. I remember this reference to the forces across the Tiber:
But those behind cried forward And those before cried back And backward now and forward Wavers the deep array.
The Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) has been talking about the old guard and the new guard. Perhaps it is not that in the Liberal Party, but a rear guard and a front guard. The rear guard wants to go forward and the front guard wants to go back. I do not know; it is not for me to decide.
I notice one place in the budget address where the Minister of Finance came very close to modesty and suggested that there were some questions for which he did not know the answers. I refer to his statement at page 432 of Hansard for Monday, April 26 when he said:
It is evident, however, that more needs to be done in financing higher education in Canada, though just what should be done and in what way are unresolved questions.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This is a statement of invitation for suggestions, and some hon. Members of the House have put forward very useful and helpful suggestions. The seriousness of the subject cannot be overestimated. As the Minister of Forestry said in his famous Bowmanville speech, "Education was and still is the key to everything else." To that part of his speech I subscribe completely. Much more must be done in all the categories which the Minister mentioned on budget night-technical and vocational training-(that great project of the ingenuity of the hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Starr)) university grants, loans to
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie C.M.H.C. for building student residences and grants for scientific research. Much more must be done in all these fields. We all recognize this. The figures setting out what we are doing are seemingly large, yet they amount to only about one third of 1 per cent of the total of our federal spending.
One field is open to immediate improvement. There should be a quick alteration of the figure relating to university grants. It will not be necessary to await the Bladen report or anything else. The grant per capita must be raised from $2 to $3 to bring it somewhere near modern needs. I was impressed by the speech of the hon. lady from Saskatoon (Mrs. Jones) the other day. She drew attention to something that is very important, namely that university grants are geared to the population of the country, which grows by about 2 per cent a year, while university expenditures are related to the university population which is soaring at the rate of 11 or 12 per cent a year. The figures with regard to this are challenging. Grants in 1962-63 amounted to $26,300,000. In 1964-65 they were $27,264,000. This does not represent a substantial rise because these amounts are geared to population. However, the number of students in the universities rose in that period from 88,751 to 113,111, so the amount per student actually declined from $297 to $241 a year.
I have a brief statement here, Mr. Speaker, showing figures for all the Provinces. If I were to be given unanimous consent to have this inserted in Hansard, it might be helpful.

speechtext:
I hear one of my hon. friends suggesting I should table the whole speech. However, I believe that is a refinement confined to the House of Representatives in the United States. Whether or not they accomplish more there than we do in this Parliament I do not care to investigate, in case I should arrive at a conclusion which is not favourable to us.
The problem to which I have referred is an urgent one and I am glad so many hon. Members have mentioned it during this discussion. Even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) referred to it. We in the Maritimes face it in a particularly acute way because so many of the students at our fine institutions come from parts of Canada other than the Atlantic region. This shows their good judgment, but it leads to severe demands on the administrators of our universities. Nova Scotia has been referred to by the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). We in Prince Edward Island require an immediate expansion of our facilities because we, too, are facing a serious problem. I should like to suggest that a special program of assistance for the Maritimes based on the same kind of thinking that went into the Atlantic Provinces Adjustment grant in

1957 should be put forward in relation to this important field of human resources, the training of our young people. This would be an ad hoc, interim step. Then there should be further moves to bring the full strength of the nation into this drive to develop our human resources. I am sure the people of Canada are pragmatic and practical enough to be able to find the means of massing the resources of the nation on behalf of education without any painful trespass upon Provincial rights. I am told the opting out formula, about which there has been much discussion and misunderstanding, might be adapted as a useful vehicle for this vital operation of national self-help for, as the President of the University of Toronto, the second greatest university in Canada, said in Halifax the other day:
These are days when abnormal growth without adequate nourishment may lead to a pernicious intellectual anemia that not even the splendors of the Expo ('67) can conceal.
This I believe was before the torch was put out.
I said earlier that my speech like Gaul would be in three parts. I should like now to refer to something the Minister said early in his speech with reference to the Govern-
May 4, 1965	COMMONS
merit's economic objectives, as the hon. gentleman called them. To use his words, "we wanted a better regional balance in both employment and growth". I say to him, or I would say to him if he were here, that he has no reason to assume that this has been attained. Far from it. In the Atlantic region of Canada unemployment is twice as high as it is in the rest of Canada, and our per capita income still lags about one third behind the rest of the country. The latest D.B.S. figures show that as of February 20, 1965, the unemployment figure for the Atlantic region was 13 per cent. In the previous year it was only 12.7 per cent. Thus, while there was a decline nationally the figure for our region actually rose in the one year period. The latest statistics we have show the figure for all of Canada, the Canadian average, standing at 5.6 per cent. Incidentally, this compares not so favourably with the 3 per cent to which the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) referred this afternoon as being one of the goals, and a good goal, of the Economic Council. However, the national average is 5.6 per cent, while unemployment in the Atlantic region stands at 13 per cent. It is in this light we should consider the statement that "we wanted a better regional balance in both employment and growth."
Are we in the Atlantic region to accept a situation where one in eight of our people are to be considered as chronically unemployed, with no hope but to move to other areas such as Toronto where the figure is 3.1 per cent? I have not heard lately whether the Minister still believes, as he did when he put forward the report of the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects, that our travel to one of these better-off areas should be subsidized.
I submit that in Prince Edward Island this Government has done things which have been positively harmful to the employment situation. The closing of H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte, a fine new building, naturally had its effect. The drying out of sub-contracts for the Enamel and Heating plant in Charlottetown caused unemployment which was significant and painful to that city and the surrounding areas. I notice that even in the realm of administration we are losing employment, jurisdiction for lighthouses in the Charlottetown marine district having been transferred to the Newfoundland district. We require now, as we have done for some time, massive help and a higher priority

The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie than has been given since the days of 1957 and 1958 when special grants were made available, when special interest was taken in a part of the country that had long undergone economic disadvantages, many of them resulting from the location of the region, and many indeed from Confederation itself.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The Government and the Prime Minister are sometimes criticized for imitating the Americans in their war on poverty. I do not think we need worry about such imitations; we have been doing it for a long time. I would suggest that they imitate them still further, launch something like the Appalachian blitzkrieg, and try to deal with some of our long standing, Atlantic economic injustices. In a spirit of helpfulness, Mr. Speaker, I will suggest one or two things which they might do. I would suggest that they start moving surely, swiftly and authoritatively by way of an announcement and commitment in regard to the construction of the Prince Edward Island causeway. I would suggest that they start moving, too, on the corridor road, which would do a tremendous job in improving-

speechtext:
I think the hon. Member realizes the hour, Mr. Speaker; but when my time is up I will be delighted to entertain his question. I think it is known how much the corridor road would do to diminish our transportation difficulties. The State of Maine is interested, the Province of New Brunswick is interested, the Province of Quebec is interested. Would it not be a helpful thing if some agency of the Federal Government showed some interest? Perhaps even a royal commission could be appointed, since there is such a proclivity toward such activities.
I say, too, that we must take some action in the Maritimes with regard to the small farming areas. I think these areas of the Maritimes are, as I have stated, ideal for an expansionary and imaginative program under ARDA. Let us put this into action. I would make a practical suggestion. The Minister made reference to it the other night in connection with the storage facilities for grain, and it is to be found at page 436 of Hansard. Those who grow grain are important. Those who grow potatoes are also important. They, too, build storage facilities. They, too, could be given the same kind of useful consideration that was mentioned. That will be helpful to the in-
May 4, 1985

The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie dustry, and I would suggest that this consideration be given.
If the hour were not so advanced, Mr. Speaker, I would give the Government many suggestions, because I do not believe in keeping good ideas to our own side of the House. Since I am long in faith and perhaps shorter in experience, I send them over in the hope that they will be acted upon. It is easy for Maritimers to talk about Maritime rights; we have done it for so long-but any nation is only as strong as its several parts. Confederation was many things; but one that it was, surely, Mr. Speaker, was the sharing of advantages and disadvantages, economic and other kinds. All our disadvantages do not stem from the Act of 1867, or 1873 in the case of my Province; but some of them do. I say this, not in a partisan sense at all, but the people of our region gained new hope in 1957 when in this era efforts were made by the national Government to redress century-old wrongs, to turn the attention of the whole nation to one of its parts which required special consideration, if only under the concept of long-delayed justice.
Perhaps, although we Maritimers are very wise, so other people say, we lost some of our initiative in the early days, when I consider the way in which we who were in at the very beginnings saw the expansion of all the other Provinces up into the vast northland and we, whose boundaries were complete at the time, sat by and let this happen. Indeed, if one would look at the map of 1867 he would see the boundaries of the then four Provinces; and if we look at what has happened since then we might find that from geography would come a lot of political and sociological truths that we should have seen long ago. It is very rarely in this House of Commons that anyone has ever looked upon this. We talk about the resources and the development of the North, but our people were also involved in the development of these things. So when we asked for subsidies, when we asked for considerations such as those that were given in 1957, we approached the national Government, not as mendicants, not as suppliants but as people who saw in the Confederation process a constant need for readjustment, for a new look, for rearrangement, for the old fashioned word that seems not so popular now-equalization -and a recognition of fiscal ability and fiscal need. These were the kind of things that were talked about in the days of the Rowell-Sirois investigation. Now the cliche seems 
to be co-operative federalism, which is interesting and important, if we all know what it means. I say it is the role of the national Government to move courageously and wisely to bring about something like economic equality of opportunity for all Canadians.
There is one final, very important part of my talk, Mr. Speaker. No nation can be strong economically if it is weak politically. Economic institutions are grounded upon the political institutions, and it is only right and proper that Members, such as the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) and others, should look in this debate at some of the great questions facing our political institutions, and into our political society itself. We live in an era of the denigration of Parliament, of excessive Provincialism, of uncertain and lacklustre national leadership. The B and B Commission talks about a crisis in our relations. Many Canadians are genuinely concerned, the thoughtful ones at least, as to whether the cohesive forces in our country are sufficient to hold us together; and they would be very imperceptive if they were not concerned. It requires that we look at the national scene, that we look at our problems and that we do not anaesthetize them by platitudes on the one hand, nor on the other scarifying them or irritating them by chauvinism or sectionalism.
Many of us have been greatly stirred, greatly encouraged, by what is referred to as the social revolution in the great, old Province of Quebec. Many of us, too, have seen the increased voice of Quebec's leaders in national affairs. Many of us have been stirred to a new consciousness by some of the problems they face. It was a shocking thing, for instance, that our great manual, Beauchesne, written by, I presume, a French Canadian, should for years have gone through edition after edition never having been translated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said before dinner, I am one of those who is dedicated to doing everything possible to assist in every way possible French Canada to attain a more meaningful and fuller place in Confederation, one prepared to recognize the justice of complaints and value and virtue of the grievances which the leaders of French Canada rightly bring to the attention of the nation as a whole. I would not wish to prolong the two solitudes approach to the fulfilment of our national destiny. I think the expression "two solitudes" is an apt one-a sadly apt one. I will never support, by word or deed, that which in modern and somewhat unsavory jargon can be called the backlash. I would rather end my modest political career immediately and forever than be a party to such a nation-destroying and Can-ada-defeating role or attitude. I believe that a better Quebec means a greater Canada.
I take second place to no Member from English speaking Canada in my desire to learn to understand and to know the problems of our fellow Canadians whose language is French and whose background is different from mine. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I would be less than candid if I did not say that, out of the wellspring of my feeling in this regard, I am troubled by some recent developments in that area of French Canada. My anxiety exists, not because of the reaction of extremists nor the extreme actions of the terrorists, nor from the violence of isolated incidents, nor the exasperated minority which preach a drastic form of separatism. Anyone who knows Canadian history knows that down through the years we have had separatists and we have had some occasional violence. My political ancestors of 1849, threw unpleasant objects at the Queen's Viceroy, Lord Elgin. This was followed up with the suggestion that we should join the United States. Some of the people of that day became politicians, while others went into something
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie better, or more lucrative, and became brewers. We had Joseph Howe, who was determined to lead Nova Scotia out of Confederation; and 20 years later we had Fielding who worked his way into power by pledging that Nova Scotia would go out. Of course, this did not follow. British Columbia was somewhat restless in those early days. It is not only British Columbia of 1965 that was controversial. We on the Island were still for keeping on the cautious side, but at one time we used to say that if we had our chance to move out tomorrow, we would take it. We have, however, never taken the drastic action of doing that.
My anxiety is not with extremists, but with those who claim to be the moderates. I want to help build a bridge of understanding, but one cannot build a bridge of understanding if the opposite bank disappears. I am troubled and concerned about recent utterances from responsible people in Quebec who suggest that the activities and jurisdictions, well established in the national field, should be pre-empted by Provincial authority. I read that the Minister of Labour suggested that unemployment and the placing of workers should become a Provincial responsibility. The equality of job opportunities for all Canadians I think is an essential of the good society and of a united Canada.
I read where Mr. Eric Kierans suggested that there will be a terrific battle at the forthcoming Provincial-Federal conference over Ottawa's banking policies. I would urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), for once in his life, to be firm and hold to his opinion regarding the necessity of financial institutions of this kind being national institutions.
I read also about housing being assumed, by the appropriate Minister, as being an exclusive field of opportunity for the Province of Quebec. We all have heard the utterances, and I hope they were misquotes and overstatements, of the education Minister in reference to treaty rights for the Province of Quebec.
I do not think any of us, and least of all I, would want to diminish by one jot or tittle the rights of the Province of Quebec. It is a great Province, and in many ways a unique Province but we cannot go on diminishing the national entity and continue as a great national state.
We want the people of French Canada to have their full say. We want to hear their grievances, and they do have some. We want
922	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Macquarrie a partnership, but if in place of a partnership we find that there are those leaders in responsible positions who prefer not a partnership, not equality, but withdrawal, it makes it painfully difficult for those who want to do nothing more than extend the hand of fellowship and the hand of friendship to try and compensate for past failures, misunderstandings and inequities, and there have been some. We want to move forward together and recognize that there are economic inequities which Quebec has suffered. As a Maritimer, I have great understanding of what Quebec has gone through. They have not received their proper share in many fields. There must be a united effort in this regard.
I have described myself in this House before, and I retain that description of myself, as an anti-separatist. Let us move closer together. Let us discuss these problems. Let us not say that at this time of national sensitivity there should be pre-emption of more and more fields by Provincial authority. Perhaps economically Quebec can pre-empt these fields, but other provinces cannot. Other provinces do not wish to do so. What will become of the great national entity if one significant part of it, no matter what its culture or language-(that is not the significant aspect of this discussion)-decides to go it alone? I suppose no one would think of stopping anyone from going it alone, although Nova Scotia found some years ago that it could not.

I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will be more forthcoming than he has been before in his reports of discussions with the Premier of Quebec. 1 hope that the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), unique as it was in its clarity and decisiveness, will serve as a standard around which this Government will rally, not in coercion, not in narrowness but as an expression of Canadianism, of nation building and of clarity in this important phase when provincialism in my opinion is rampant and the national identity gravely undermined. Dean Maxwell Cohen wrote in today's Gazette:

viding, however, that there are safeguards to Federal Canada as the only "sovereign" Canadian state known to the world-and to France. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even if we had the opportunity to do so, our party would not introduce any amendment to the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) on his annual financial statement, since we do not believe that such a procedure would be conducive to the expansion of the Canadian economy. It would be a negative gesture that would only serve the political aspirations, often unspeakable, of those who use them.
I intend to analyse briefly various provisions of this budget and also to expose the hypocrisy shown by certain opposition parties in this house during the budget debate.
I would like to deal first with this last suggestion which is rather humorous and would not bear the cold analysis of the figures presented in the budget.
Last night we had the opportunity to vote on a motion of non-confidence introduced by the Conservative party. As you already know, we members of the Social Credit party have, as a group, supported the present government. Before this vote was taken we had made known our intention to support the government because we do not believe in the outmoded procedure used by the various opposition parties every time they have the opportunity to do so.
It is strange to note that during a previous vote a large majority of Conservative members were absent from the house because they did not know if at least one of the opposition parties would support the government so it would not be defeated. But yesterday the situation was different, because we had made it known that we would support
May 4, 1965
the government. We saw in the house most Conservative members who did not hesitate to vote against the government and jeered at us because we were supporting it.
I feel that is the most obvious display of chronic hypocrisy from the old guard politicians with regard to the administration of this country's business, which they neglect to make fantastic turnabouts. Had there not been seven responsible opposition members in the house last night the government would have been toppled by a vote of 107 to 104 and today, we would be in the midst of an election campaign.
It is not an election campaign which would have been disastrous but the discomfiture of those government and opposition members who want anything but an election. The Canadian people are certainly not interested in going back to the polls in the present circumstances, and I wonder what political parties in the house at the present time would be bold and daring enough to pretend that they would gain public support should an election be called in the near future.
If, on the occasion of the budget debate, we go into a detailed study of our political situation, starting with the party in office, we readily realize that the Liberals have not had time to recover from the scandal brought forward by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and that they find themselves with quite an awkward cabinet. Then, they were immediately compelled to get rid of the youngest minister whose taste for horse races compares only with Lucien Rivard's boldness. To offset such a situation at election time, the Minister of Finance should have sought inspiration from the monetary reform advocated by the Social Credit; but instead of that, he came up with a budget which is neither fowl nor fish and which in no way can make us forget the series of scandals which rocked the Liberal party.
The situation is even more ludicrous within the Conservative party which has been singing for some time now a modern version of an old song. The omnipotent Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) continues to lose his grip on Canada where, in his opinion, the province of Quebec is no longer existent but where candidates from all quarters are lining up to take over a leadership which, because of him, has become pitiful. If the present Leader of the Opposition is serious when he is clamouring for an election in order to instil new life in the country's economy, then it is more serious than I
The Budget-Mr. Cha-pdelaine thought, for I would say this is a sadistic attitude. It is really sadistic to want to drag down with him all that remains of a career which ceased to glitter a long time ago.
Perhaps the New Democratic party was hoping for an election before it realized that the Conservative party had left in Ontario a vacuum which it can no longer hope to fill because the voters would probably elect independent candidates who would be a better reflection of the parliamentary image of integrity which all Canadians expect from politicians. I think that the New Democratic party, by associating itself with old-line parties when voting on non-confidence motions and also by its absenteeism when they could not forecast the results of the vote, has fallen into the trap of parliamentary hypocrisy and that the people will not forget it.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
It is very hard for me to find a reason which would justify the attitude of the Creditistes on those non-confidence motions, since this group of men, that I cannot call a party, has not been elected as such, this grouping of men, as I say, has lost ground m the province of Quebec and there is no hope for them to be re-elected to this house.
As for us, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that we are the only ones who acted responsibly by supporting the government and by avoiding an election that would have settled none of the problems which we must face in this parliament and which we want to solve for the benefit of all Canadians. I think this attitude of responsible men who refuse to indulge in childish games, like the one served on us in the form of non-confidence motions, will be recognized by the people and appreciated throughout Canada.
I cannot help but mention that I saw a number of happy faces among the members of the opposition after the vote last night. It is not due to any lack of admiration, but rather out of sheer embarrassment, that they refrained from showing us openly their deepest gratitude.
While we do not think that such non-confidence motions are apt to improve the admiration of Canadians, we feel that it is essential to make positive suggestions so that, in the next budget, they may be taken into consideration and even implemented, if it is found advisable.
The budget announces a 10 per cent income tax reduction which is completely inadequate and does not benefit the lower brackets.

May 4, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Chapdelaine
If, instead of granting a 10 per cent tax reduction at the present level, the government had increased the exemptions to $4,000 for married people and to $2,000 for single persons, this would have affected all that low income category where such tax reductions are really needed, and this would have been the first step in the war on poverty that the government plans to launch in the near future.
To meet the deficit involved by such a decision without causing any dislocation, the government could easily have raised the tax scale for those earning over $4,000 a year, because they are not as acutely affected by the iniquity of a too heavy tax burden.
There were some other commendable proposals in this budget, such as the Canada Development Corporation, patterned after the General Investment Corporation of the province of Quebec and I commend the Minister of Finance for having taken from Quebec another brilliant idea of which we are capable. I am sure that all Canadians will be proud and happy to become shareholders in such a corporation, because they will have the satisfaction of participating in the development of our country and in the investment of Canadian capital on Canadian soil.
There are also the other measures respecting foreign periodicals and newspapers, agriculture, industry, scientific research, etc., all of which contain some good and which we will be proud to support after discussing them in this house.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall that on the occasion of such a budget speech last year, I had directed to the Minister of Finance a question which remained unanswered. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) did not have time to answer, or was afraid to answer or if it was merely through unconcern for the financial problems this country is now facing, in short, I do not know the reasons why he did not even deign to show interest.
He is undoubtedly aware that the service of the Canadian debt has now reached the unprecedented level of $1,100 million, which represents a $62 million increase for the last fiscal year, and I do not see anything announced in the budget to correct this alarming situation.
It is quite normal that when one borrows money, one must pay the interest to his lender when it is in the field of private enterprise. But when the government borrows for public investment purposes, that is for

non-productive investments, why does not the Minister of Finance think of finding the necessary credit to finance public utility investments on which he should not have to pay any interest since the investments themselves do not yield anything.
It would be very easy for the Bank of Canada to create new credit for the implementation of those public utility projects, in proportion to the amounts required for investment in that field and without the government having to pay the bank any interest on the credit thus created.
To prevent that supplementary credit from giving rise to inflation, the Minister of Finance would just have to tell the Bank of Canada to reduce the margin of credit the chartered banks are allowed to create on the basis of their deposits with the central bank, in other words, to reduce the amount of credit available to private enterprise in proportion to the increase in credit for public utility purposes.
That way there would be no inflation, we would no longer have to pay interest on new loans and, gradually, we could get rid of those debt charges which now amount to $1,100 million.
That is the suggestion I made to the Minister of Finance last year and I repeat what I said at that time: If you can prove that my proposals do not make sense, then I shall refrain from making such recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday of last week all Canadians the least bit interested in politics were wondering what would be in the budget now under consideration in the house. I did not find therein all I would have wished for, but I realize the complex nature of a budget which affects every Canadian.

What did the Canadian people expect from the budget? What made them say that such a change, such an improvement, such a tax cut was needed? It is quite normal that the general public should judge a budget according to what they get from it or what it takes from them. However, an increase or a reduction in direct or indirect taxes must not be made without taking into account the general economy.
Canada, especially in the last few years, has experienced a fast economic growth which will continue-according to every forecast- and this will benefit the population as a whole.

I am very happy to note that growth which,
I hope, will be beneficial not only to one segment but to the whole population.
It is a growth budget, they say. I rather think that this is the prominent feature of the budget, since it fosters great hope for the establishment of new industries, especially in less favoured areas, for some special assistance to industries already established in underdeveloped areas, for an increase in capital invested in various concerns, in short we hope that the whole economy, especially the farming area, will benefit from that growth and we expect an immediate effort in order to alleviate hardship prevailing in some areas of the country.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that all possible and special attention will be paid those underdeveloped areas and that efforts will be centred toward reorganizing the economy of those areas where the people do not yet take advantage or full advantage of this expansion we have been hearing so much about for a few months.
We are told that, throughout the country, the income and the standard of living are increasing rapidly, that there is considerable industrial development and that unemployment is decreasing. That is what we hear, that is being repeated, particularly of late.
Evidently, that is the case as far as the majority of the population is concerned; none the less, thousands of families in the poorer areas are frustrated, and it is high time that they enjoy this economic growth and that they do not feel as if they were forgotten Canadian families.
That is also the case of the whole region I have the honour to represent, particularly the northern part of this country and other adjoining counties, where a short visit would suffice to convince some of those responsible for putting these policies forward to forget their theories which they seem to consider as corollaries. Certain general reports coupled with some statistics may seem to indicate that a given situation is really what we think it is. However, a closer examination, for instance of the true average income of farm workers and others, in a given area, will readily show that the average income may be very low. Obviously, it is then necessary to adjust the economy of such areas where the people as a whole, and rightly so, seem to wonder if they are not really being ignored.
There is obviously quite an imbalance be-

Mr. Speaker, I feel it is essential to point out the needs of those who chose us to represent them, especially when their situation is as precarious as it is at present.
It is true, as I read in a newspaper last week, that certain members are entirely taken up by regional problems, by the great number of letters and representations they receive. I readily admit it, and I agree also that more time would have to be spent on research and study, on the country's business in general and on all government measures submitted to the house.
However, as I said earlier, at the risk of being accused of provincialism and regionalism I feel duty bound to point out the problems of my riding as far as possible.
I must also add that several hours could be saved each week if some government employees were a little more impartial and objective in dealing with requests made to them.
I had a few remarks to make on that matter but I will skip them to deal with another subject.
May 4, 1965

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly about national unity, a matter which is of interest to all Canadians worthy of that name.
I must say, and this is my personal opinion, that in our first years in elementary school our teachers give us an idea of the incidents which marked the beginning of Canada, with all the dates, names, battles, etc. to remember. From what I learned, the French were good and the English bad. How many happy or unhappy scenes have passed through the mind of each of us, depending, of course, on the good or bad results of these battles described sometimes quite vigorously.
On reading some of the history books on Canada available to school children of the provinces other than Quebec, I have had the impression that our heroes were just the opposite on the English side.
It is therefore logical for one to ask himself to what extent the views of many Canadians, which are absolutely contradictory in many cases, are due to a teaching of history which is partial and prejudiced from the start.
I do not want to cast any reflection on the teachers of that time, because I had excellent teachers even if they may seem to have had little success with me. I merely wish to stress the need for every Canadian to reconsider objectively his own concept of Canada, as it now stands as a whole. History is one of the most humanizing disciplines, but it is a science where objectivity must enable everyone to realize that Canada was founded by very worthy men who came from France, England and other countries. One must recognize that Intendant Bigot's self-centredness was just as despicable as Lord Durham's attitude and conclusions.
Today, all those conflicts of the past, all that one-way teaching of the history of Canada seem to break to the surface. We are facing a tense and disturbing situation the implications of which extend well beyond the policy of such a party aiming first of all at having re-elected the largest possible number of members. Before such a situation, the latter attitude must be forgotten. Which attitude should we take? What should we do? Blame one another? Quarrel? Fight or try to understand one another?
I believe sincerely that our problem of unity is one of misunderstanding. We do not know one another well enough. Many, even members of the elite, jump to conclusions on the basis of incomplete information, just as many declare themselves for or against, while they do not even know the first thing about a
The Budget-Mr. Laverdiere democratic system, while they only have very elementary knowledge of their history, of the economy of their province or their country and all consequences resulting from extremist attitudes.
One thing is sure. French Canadians were very docile, very submissive after the defeat of 1759, too submissive perhaps in spite of the understanding and good-will shown by most leaders of that time. Our forefathers cooperated, even if some reports state otherwise, such as this one on the American invasion of 1775-76 which says about the people of Beaumont: "Except for five or six good subjects, that parish (Beaumont) relished very much the spirit of the rebellion."
French Canadians co-operated at the time of the abovementioned invasion; we cooperated in 1812 right after the vexatious measures taken by Craig; we co-operated in 1842; we co-operated in 1848; we co-operated in 1867; we co-operated in 1914; we co-operated in 1939. We have always co-operated.
We made concessions time after time; in addition to all these concessions, which one do you think we have not made that we should have? But what did we gain by that? A few crumbs, such as bilingual cheques, bilingual currency, bilingual stamps and a few other minor things.
It makes you wonder what is left for us to do after 98 years within confederation. What stand should we take? What should we do now to unite our country? What else should we concede?
The time for concessions is past, it is time now to substitute for that policy of co-operation a policy of give and take, based on equality and dignity. We extend our hand, as we have always done, but it is a firm and resolute hand. We have been co-operating long enough, perhaps with some apathy, in order to maintain peace.
We no longer intend to beg for unity; we wish to be treated on an equal footing to arrive to an official recognition of our presence, of what we are and represent. Mutual understanding is necessary, but I am convinced that we can only attain it provided a concession on our part is met by a similar concession on the other part.
I sincerely believe that French Canadians can no longer be satisfied with half-measures and a few crumbs. Such an aspiration is very natural and legitimate.
Quebec is a French Canadian state whose rights as defined in the 1867 Act must be respected. We have become an adult people,

May 4, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Nielsen decolonized at last and conscious of our dignity, and we want nothing else but to be masters in our own house.
A strong people is above all a united people, and therefore a people which respects the deepest aspirations of each of its fellow citizens.

Mr. Speaker, we are now considering the federal budget, only a very short while after having examined the speech from the throne. Indeed, the speech from the throne, which was read on April 5, had a rather unusual characteristic, at least as far as the government was concerned, because the latter has come to realize that there is poverty in Canada and has declared its intention of waging war on poverty. Consequently, we were anxious to get to April 26, that is 21 days later, to hear what kind of a budget the Minister of Finance would present and what kind of legislation he would propose to fight poverty in Canada.
Contrary to the speech from the throne, however, the budget speech showed us that far from waging war on poverty, the government keeps picking on Canadians who are destitute. It wages war on the poor and not on poverty, because it is not with a tax reduction of $3 per year for a father of a family who has two dependants and who earns $3,000-a reduction of about $3 a year or a little less than one cent a day-that one can fight poverty in Canada. That budget will create even more poor people, will even mass-produce them, if I may use that expression.
While in Ottawa a lot was being said about poverty, about two days after the speech from the throne, the Quebec government announced that various taxes were being increased. Poverty is discussed in Ottawa and taxes are increased in Quebec. That is an instance of co-operative federalism which we are asked to swallow. It is probably the kind of co-operative federalism which, according to the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), is to be found between trusteeship federalism and confederative federalism. For the Secretary of State, co-operative federalism is to be found between two chairs- and let us say in passing that he knows a lot about furniture. While poverty is discussed in Ottawa, taxes are discussed in Quebec.
The present Quebec government, which can be compared with that of Ottawa, has levied 87 kinds of new taxes since 1960. Nevertheless, we had been told at that time that the government would administer the province without any increase in taxation. Has the premier of that province been playing on words or did he intend to administer the province with a 22S20-60
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau hundred kinds of new taxes. If such is the case, he would lack only 13 of them to reach his goal.
Instead of fighting poverty in Canada, our government is trying to help the poor in other countries, especially those in England. Did we not grant a $268 million loan without interest to the Bank of England in order to save the pound sterling? But to save the needy in Canada, they will continue to invent all possible kinds of taxes. To help others, let us burden our own people. That is what the government seem to be saying. They maintain their policy of trying to help the poor in foreign countries rather than those who have difficulties in our own country, Canada, a country so rich in production, in natural resources, in all kinds of things but where, according to the speech from the throne, poverty is to be found.
Looking into this mirror held up to facts, in the face of poverty in Canada and considering the wealth of resources of this country, we see in the last budget speech, no solution to deal with this problem, to attack or change the financial system or to correct the financing system, because of which the production is not geared to consumption.
This evening I should especially like to develop one point which the Minister of Finance laboured for quite a while in his budget speech, namely public capital. Because for quite a long time we of the Ralliement Creditiste have been stating that there is an enormous difference between social capital, or public capital, and private capital.
Private capital is a productive capital. It is a capital that can be invested in an industry, in a private enterprise. Production can be made with such capital, and with such production, profits can be made, and out of those profits, interest can be paid. On the other hand, there is also a public capital. That capital does not produce; it does not yield anything to anybody, it does not bring any return to the community, to the Canadians as a whole. And today with our present finance system everything is confused. No difference is made between private and public capital. No attention is paid to the difference between the two. The worst nonsense is that people realize now that public capital is a danger to private capital.
When bridges, roads, schools, sidewalks, sewer systems, waterworks or any public capital development which belongs to everybody is built, it produces nothing, because a school cannot produce a school after ten
May 4. 1965

The Budget-Mr. Rondeau years, nor a bridge produce another bridge after 15 or 20 years, and it is the same for a road. This capital does not yield anything.
Then, why does our present financial system compel society, when we build bridges, roads, schools, sidewalks, waterworks or any public social development, to pay three, four, five, seven and ten times for that public capital, while it has been produced only once?
It is a mathematical nonsense, and that is where our present financial system is un-arithmetieal, unscientific, while the Social Credit system which we advocate would put the Bank of Canada at the service of public capital, of social capital, at the disposal of our public institutions so that they could realize their development of public capital without compelling individuals to pay five, six, seven, eight and even ten times for those achievements.

I was talking recently with a staunch Liberal who was saying that taxes were increasing every day and every year and once I had shown him the comparison between social capital and private capital, he agreed with me.
Nowadays the sidewalks, bridges, waterworks and sewer systems in our municipalities and cities cost more, after a number of years, than the houses near which they are built.
The sidewalks that are built are paid 15 and 20 times over. The Jacques Cartier bridge was built a few years ago. Its cost was paid more than 20 times over through interest and the debt still exists in the books; as a matter of fact, it is part or our national debt.
Why is it that our sidewalks, our bridges, our highways, our sewer systems and our schools cost so much nowadays? It is due to the fact that we do not have any financing system in the public sector. We make no distinction between public capital and private capital. Why cannot our municipalities, our school boards borrow from the Bank of Canada, by way of bonds, the sums required for their development? Those sums would then be repaid to the Bank of Canada according to the depreciation of our public developments. The credit of the Bank of Canada, under Creditiste principles, would be put into circulation in terms of the development in the public sector.
For instance, if we built a school costing a million dollars, a credit of $1 million would be granted to the school board concerned in

order to build its school. If according to the engineers, the school would last 20 years, the Bank of Canada would be reimbursed at a rate of $50,000 per year. This means that at the end of 20 years the total debt, or the cost of the public capital involved, would have been repaid.
But today it takes 25, 30, 40 or 50 years to pay for a school, so that by then it is obsolete. The same thing applies to roads unfit for traffic and for bridges no longer in existence; yet, the amount of public capital involved still figures in our national debt.
The present structure of our financial system, according to the Creditistes, will in the long run completely destroy the public financial sector and reduce by 100 per cent the value of money in Canada. Why? Because the federal government, responsible for the administration of public affairs, has no financial system to satisfy the many needs for public capital in the country. The only thing they can do, and they do it, is to borrow from the United States. They borrow in Europe and everywhere in the world, or from Canadian chartered banks.
They borrow from private institutions to develop the public sector and that is why we claim that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will be required through legislation and with the assistance of a credit commission, to make credit a social proposition, if you wish. In other words, public capital will have to be made available to companies at administrative cost, because today public capital is destroying private capital due to taxes that are going up constantly; indebtedness is increasing. In fact, the interest on the public debt this year will exceed $1 billion. Why? To pay interest to private institutions, to banks, because they have advanced to the government of our nation the necessary credit to permit the development of the public sector. On the other hand, under the Social Credit doctrine the federal government could use the Bank of Canada to put credit in circulation or withdraw it according to the depreciation of public developments.
That is where our system is scientific. We put money or credit in circulation according to the existing guarantees or values. Instead of assuming obligations toward other countries to bring money to Canada, we could assume commitments toward the Bank of Canada to put our credit in circulation, according to the development of our country, and take money out of circulation according
May 4, 1965

to the consumption of our public production, to the depreciation of our social capital.
If we are unwilling to stop and see that our financial system itself is carrying a cancer, we will not succeed in finding a way out. If the federal government insists on leaving the control of finance and credit in the hands of individuals, namely eight private undertakings which are the banks, it is obvious that those private undertakings called banks will ruin the country and also the savings of individuals and investors.
It is ridiculous that sidewalks, sewers and roads built in front of our houses should cost more than the houses themselves. None the less, that is the present situation, which proves that our financial system is archaic, out-dated and out-moded. That is why members of Parliament should awaken, should stop playing politics and tackle the only real problem which exists in Canada-finance.
We are wasting time in this house in trying to find solutions. We are looking in the wrong places to find money for the administration of the country. Yet, it was Mr. Mackenzie King, the former Prime Minister of Canada, who said:
Give me control over money and credit of a nation and I need not care about its lawmakers.
The statement made by Mr. Mackenzie King in 1935 is still true today. Those who control our financial system do not care about us, in this house. Why? Because, as far as they are concerned, we are only makers of laws that will bring interest to those who hide behind the bank counters and who make money as they see fit and as much as they want.
If they decide one day to bring about prosperity in Canada, they put billions of dollars in circulation, but the day after, if they decide to restrict credit, they declare that money is scarce. Then businesses become shaky and bankruptcies increase. Why? Because a group of individuals have been allowed to control our finance and they can do as they please, because the Minister of Finance fails to assume his responsibilities, having been elected by those who actually control finance behind their counters.
That is why we, in this corner of the house, are shocked at the position taken by the Liberal party which pretends to fight poverty but keeps on maintaining a financial system likely to mass-produce poor people, because the exemptions announced in the budget will still favour the rich at the expense of the poor.

Mr. Speaker, if hon. members could be serious for a moment, they would consider our suggestion. If there are other suggestions, let them be made without delay so that our city problems may be settled. In fact, I know of towns in the eastern townships, in the province of Quebec and elsewhere in Canada, where nearly 65 or 70 per cent of the municipal budget is assigned to interest on the municipal debt. There remains only 20 or 25 per cent to be spent on waterworks, police services, in brief on municipal services. Some 65 to 70 per cent of the budget is used to pay the interest on municipal debts while we, in this house, could enable our public bodies and municipalities to obtain the necessary public capital and to pay the cost once only.
Mr. Speaker, we, from the Ralliement Creditiste, do not say that we will give schools to everybody, that we will build roads without having to pay for them. We do not say that we will build sidewalks and that we will have nothing to pay for that. We never said that. We always stated that the Bank of Canada should issue credit in keeping with public development and remove it from circulation according to public consumption.
If a bridge costs a million dollars and will last 20 years, we should remove $50,000 a year from circulation over 20 years; after 20 years the bridge would be depreciated and the debt would be paid. Under this system we would have paid once for our public capital, our schools, our sewers and our sidewalks. But under the present financial system, we pay the cost of one school for us against the cost of five schools to finance companies.
We pay the cost of one road for us and that of five or ten roads to the financiers. We pay the cost of one sidewalk for us and that of ten to the financiers. And yet we get only one sidewalk, one bridge, one road. A school does not multiply at the end of the year, nor does a road or a bridge.
If public capital is non-productive capital, if social capital does not benefit anyone, why force the Canadian people to pay 10, 15 and even 20 times their public capital?
That explains why our public debt keeps increasing; that explains most of the municipal, provincial and school board debts.
It is easy to say: Masters in our own house. But where does the money come from? From foreigners. We know that last year we gave more than $1 billion in interest to the banks.
